blocks.text: ...walking together
The “heel” procedure is suitable for all everyday situations in which we want to walk relaxed with our dog.
The training of the “heel” action described here serves to build up the basic response to this cue and to make walking on the leash as well as off-leash following reliable, motivated and relaxed.
For our dog, “heel” should be an action of finding its place, from any starting position, in a position slightly offset behind us and on the side we have trained.
“Heel” means: walking at our side reliably, motivated and relaxed.
Start, prerequisites & frequency 📋
Start: From about the 9th month of age.
Prerequisite: Our dog masters “sit” and we are positively motivated.
Training frequency: Daily during our walk in loose sequence, as it feels right – starting without distraction, over the course of the weeks under growing distraction.
Training environment & increasing stimulus level 🌿
Ideally we train “heel” on the walk in a low-stimulus, quiet environment.
Later, as responsiveness grows, training may take place as appropriate to the situation under steadily increasing stimulus levels.
The stimulus level should be raised slowly, since every training procedure should end positively and our dog must not be overwhelmed.
Step 1 – Cue & walking backwards 🔙
While walking together with the dog – especially when the dog moves out ahead – we give a calm “heeeel” and at the same time begin to walk calmly backwards.
Step 2 – Motivating backward walking 🎯
While walking backwards with motivating talk (e.g. “Good … heel”), we let our dog overtake us towards the back, with gentle leash assistance.
Step 3 – Walking forwards & turning in 🔄
As soon as the dog is behind us, we walk forwards again for 2–3 steps, repeatedly accompanying this with the cue “heel”, and let the dog follow us with gentle leash assistance.
It is very important here that our dog turns in towards us – a turn outwards is by no means to be accepted.
Step 4 – Sit & confirmation ✅
The dog following us is brought into a sit behind us with the cue “sit”. Over time this “sit” is replaced by “heel”.
Once the dog sits, it is praised – gladly also confirmed playfully.
Step 5 – Progress & withdrawing the aids 📈
Over the course of the weeks, provided the training is good, we will notice that our dog carries out the cue “heel” increasingly reliably and willingly.
As far as this progress goes, we can withdraw our leash aids step by step.
Soon our dog will gladly follow the cue “heel”, and this in turn makes walking together more pleasant.
The support from our backward and forward movement work can likewise be slowly withdrawn – the motivating talk, however, remains.

In this way our dog will learn to find its place with us on the cue “heel” – supplemented by the hand movement – both when standing and while walking, and increasingly to keep the position at our side.
What you should avoid ⚠️
Avoid sharply spoken commands in training and in everyday use.
Avoid taut pulling on the leash during execution.
Avoid turning in away from the handler during the exercise.
Avoid carrying out the exercise in a stressed or strongly distracting situation.
Practical impulse: The “five-moment round”

On your next walk, consciously choose five moments in which your dog walks slightly ahead, and carry out a complete heel procedure each time: cue, backward steps, turning in, sit, praise. Afterwards, note how purposeful the inward turn was – this is the most important quality indicator.
Did I make sure of a stress-free environment at the beginning?
Did I speak to my dog calmly?
Did I act in a motivating way?
Did I use the leash aid calmly?
Did I make sure that I walked backwards immediately?
Did I accompany the backward walking, in connection with the dog overtaking me, in a motivating way?
Did I walk backwards enough for support?
Was the leash aid present as appropriate, without stressing the dog?
Did the dog complete the turn inwards behind me and come purposefully to sit behind me?
Did I praise calmly and intensively?
